analysis.one_liner: Limits judges' ability to keep court records and settlements secret in cases involving public health or safety hazards.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have limited secret settlements in court cases involving public health and safety hazards, died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies sued over dangerous products often settle on condition that the evidence stays secret: judges issue protective orders and seal records, so the public, regulators, and future victims never learn about the hazard. This bill would change that. In any lawsuit involving facts about public health or safety, a judge could only keep information secret after making specific findings that secrecy is justified, and no settlement could block a party from reporting the hazard to a federal or state regulator. It would also let parties reveal that a settlement happened and what it covered (except the dollar amount), while preserving protection for personal identifying information and classified material. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who buy products, take prescription drugs, drive cars, and work in regulated industries. When a lawsuit uncovers a safety hazard — a defective device, a contaminated drug, a dangerous vehicle part — the bill would let that information reach regulators, journalists, and future victims instead of being buried in a confidential settlement. People who later suffer the same harm would also get access to evidence that could help their own cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, patients, and workers exposed to hazards

how_it_helps.text: Courts could no longer approve settlements that hide information about public health or safety hazards unless the judge first made specific factual findings that secrecy was justified and that the order was no broader than necessary.

Parties could always report safety hazards to federal or state regulators: the bill forbids courts from enforcing any settlement term that blocks disclosure to a government agency with enforcement authority.
Settlement terms hiding the fact of a settlement, its terms (not the dollar amount), or the underlying safety hazards would be unenforceable, so the public could learn what dangers a case revealed.

The bill balances privacy against transparency with a rebuttable presumption that an individual's personally identifiable information outweighs disclosure, and it explicitly leaves classified information untouched.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that face lawsuits over health and safety hazards — drug makers, device makers, automakers, and other product manufacturers — lose their ability to settle quietly and seal the evidence. Some would face more public scrutiny, regulatory referrals, and copycat lawsuits; some settlements would become harder to reach, raising litigation costs that can be passed to consumers in prices.

drawbacks.text: Businesses legitimately rely on confidential settlements to protect trade secrets, proprietary processes, and sensitive business information, and a rule that pushes more of that into the open could deter companies from settling meritorious claims — meaning more trials, longer cases, and higher litigation costs that can ultimately show up in prices.

Secrecy sometimes serves individuals, not companies: victims of private wrongdoing (for example in medical or family matters) often want their names and records kept out of public view. The bill responds with a rebuttable presumption that personally identifiable information outweighs the public's interest in disclosure, but a presumption is not an absolute shield and some privacy advocates would still worry about edge cases.

The bill overrides judicial discretion in a matter courts have traditionally governed through their own rules (Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(c)), which opponents would call unnecessary federal intrusion into court management — the standard counterargument raised against every version of the Sunshine in Litigation Act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: public safety information — about defective products, unsafe drugs, dangerous working conditions — is now routinely locked inside confidential settlements, and this bill would have forced courts to justify each sealing with specific findings and let regulators see what was hidden. The cost side is genuine but manageable: the bill carve-outs for personal privacy (a rebuttable presumption favoring confidentiality) and its requirement that any secrecy order be no broader than necessary were designed to preserve legitimate trade-secret and privacy protection, and courts would still have been able to keep truly sensitive information sealed upon a showing. The main honest objection is that it adds federal rules to a matter courts largely govern themselves, and could make some companies fight rather than settle, raising litigation costs that show up in prices. On balance, the transparency benefit outweighs the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to a subcommittee two weeks later, and then sat untouched until the two-year Congress ended — never marked up, never voted on.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 1, 2014 and referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee.
On April 16, 2014 it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice — the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that face lawsuits over health and safety hazards keep the ability to settle quietly and seal the evidence, because the current rules allowing secret settlements and sealed court records stay in place.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sunshine in Litigation Act of 2014 on April 1, 2014.

for.name: Rep. Ted Deutch
for.what_they_did: Joined Nadler in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred: no hearing, no markup, and no committee vote was ever scheduled, so the bill never left the subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and with no hearings or votes there is no record of any Republican support; the bill never advanced far enough for a partisan floor fight.

industries.industry: Defendants in health-and-safety litigation (drug and medical device makers, automakers, product manufacturers, insurers)
industries.note: These companies use protective orders and confidential settlements to keep evidence of product dangers out of public view and out of the hands of future plaintiffs and regulators. The bill would make that secrecy far harder to obtain, exposing them to copycat lawsuits, regulatory action, and reputational damage when a case reveals a genuine hazard.

Attorneys representing injured consumers and workers would gain leverage: once safety evidence from one case is public, it can support later cases and negotiations. This is a real industry interest that runs alongside the public's here, since the same openness that helps future victims helps their lawyers.
